label: text

Mr. Willis was 57 years old at the time of his death and is survived by a widow and six children.

text: The following seems a tribute to Mr. A. H. Barlow, Manager of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation:—The home papers publish the portrait of Sir Frank Nelson, M.P. for Stroud, as among the early arrivals at the House of Commons to hear Mr. Churchill's Budget speech. Sir Frank is the only Bangkok man in the House, says the "Bangkok Times." He was a young man in the Hongkong Bank away back in 1906 to 1910, under Mr. A. H. Barlow. He was then a bachelor, with a taste for amateur theatricals and lawn tennis. On his first leave he got married and was transferred to Bombay. He left the Bank's service and saw his future in the cotton market. In the course of time he became chairman of the Bombay Chamber of Commerce and his services in that position brought him in due time his neighborhood. Sir Frank in a letter recently acknowledged under Mr. A. E. Barlow's train when while in great use in the attributed his later successful career.

label: text
text: Lieutenant-Colonel John C. Faunthorpe, C.B.E., M.C., V.D., A.D.C., of the Southern Regiment of the United Provinces Horse at Cawnpore, is to compete at the N.R.A. meeting at Bisley in July. This officer, who has been commanding the Auxiliary Force at Lucknow, is a well-known big game and sporting rifle marksman. He captained the British team which competed at the Olympic Games in France last year. He has shot for India with the Service rifle and is the 1924 champion at the Running Deer Singles.

label: text
text: The University Council at its meeting on May 21, accepted with regret the resignation of Professor R. K. M. Simpson from the post of Associate Editor of the Union Magazine. The Vice Chancellor duly appointed Mr. George Keeton to the post. The Council on March 31 appointed Mr. Ong Chong-keng to succeed Mr. M. B. Osman as Editor of the English Section of the Magazine, and Mr. Lau Mo-tsung as Editor of the Chinese Section of the Magazine. Mr. Lau subsequently tendered his resignation, and the post was filled by Mr. Lee Pak-hung, who was appointed on June 2.

label: paragraph_title
text: ERRING WIVES.

label: text
text: THE LAW AND THE HUSBAND.

label: text
text: The Government proposes to introduce legislation to remove the liability under which a husband is at present placed for his wife's wrongdoings. This announcement was made by Viscount Cave, the Lord Chancellor, in reply to a suggestion by Lord Danesfort that a committee should be appointed to consider the necessity for an alteration in the responsibility of husbands in view of the wide legislative changes that have been made in recent years in the status and rights of married women.

label: text
text: Lord Danesfort said that the law to-day was that a husband was responsible for his wife's wrong doings, even though committed without his knowledge or consent, and although his wife was separated from him at the time. It was the survival of some of the old common law doctrines which, according to modern ideas, were crude.

label: text
text: Lord Haldane was sympathetic with "the unfortunate husband," and agreed that it was monstrous that the principle referred to by Lord Danesfort should remain.

label: text
text: Lord Darling said that this was a matter of reform that ought to be urged by women themselves if they wanted to be considered as independent people. The law assumed that a married man and woman were only one person, and therefore if the woman committed a wrong it was committed by her husband. It had been laid down, in fact, that a man's wife was in a somewhat similar position to a man's pet monkey, and that he was responsible for the mischief she committed.

label: text
text:
DOMESTIC CHASTISMENT.
The husband was, by the old law,
allowed to give his wife moderate
correction, on the ground that if
he had to answer for her mischievous behaviour the law thought
it reasonable to entrust him with

label: text
text: this power to restrain her by domestic chustisement. This power of correction began to be doubted in the reign of Charles II.

label: text
text: "If I were to put the woman's point of view," continued Lord Darling, "I am sure that they will not desire to be joined to their husbands more than is absolutely necessary. They will want to bring actions, get damages, and put them into their own pockets. The equality of the sexes demands this change in the law."

label: text
text: The Lord Chancellor, Lord Cave, replying for the Government, said that the old rule that a husband might beat his wife with a stick no thicker than his thumb had gradually disappeared, but another injustice had been caused by the retention of the liability of the husband. If the husband was liable for his wife's torts, at all events in times past he had her money, but to-day the law was that no part of the woman's property went to the husband on marriage. It was an unjust state of things.

label: text
text: "We have heard much of the rights of wives," concluded Lord Cave, "but I think in this case we ought to consider the rights of husbands." The Government proposed at a convenient time to introduce legislation, to remove this grievance, but it might not be possible to find time during the present session.
